reason: The sources thoroughly support an engaging 45-second script about escape velocity misconceptions with over ten well-supported claims.
story: You do not need to blast off at 25,000 miles per hour to escape Earth's gravity. That terrifying speed limit, known as escape velocity, is actually just a shortcut for a single unpowered burst. If you fire a projectile and let gravity do all the work, yes, you need 11.2 kilometers per second to coast into the cosmos forever. But rockets are not cannonballs. By keeping their engines burning, they can climb at a leisurely walking pace and still slip away completely. Escape velocity is not a speed limit you must break; it is merely an energy bill. And thanks to continuous thrust, you do not have to pay it all at once.
angle: You do not need to reach 25,000 miles per hour to escape Earth; any speed will work if you maintain continuous thrust.

claims.claim: Escape velocity from Earth's surface is approximately 11.2 km/s, or about 25,000 miles per hour.
Escape velocity is the minimum speed an object needs to escape a planet's gravitational field without further propulsion.
Escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the escaping object.
A rocket under continuous or intermittent thrust can attain escape at any non-zero speed.
Escape velocity is exactly sqrt(2) times the circular orbital velocity at the same radius.
The escape velocity formula can be derived from the conservation of energy by setting kinetic energy plus gravitational potential energy equal to zero.
Earth's orbital velocity at the surface or low altitude is roughly 7.8 to 7.9 km/s.
The Moon's escape velocity is about 2.38 km/s to 2.4 km/s.
Mars's escape velocity is about 5.0 km/s.
Setting escape velocity equal to the speed of light yields the Schwarzschild radius formula for a black hole: r_s = 2GM/c^2.
Escape velocity decreases with altitude as distance from the center of the body increases.
Escape velocity is a scalar speed independent of direction in a spherically symmetric body.

disputed: Slight variations in decimal places for constants like G and planetary mass values across different sources; scripts should use standard accepted rounded figures like 11.2 km/s.
